title: AG Grid Custom Editors and Filters with Select2 - Method-by-Method Walkthrough
one_line_summary: A line-by-line dissection of a custom AG Grid cell editor backed by Select2 plus a custom Portuguese-localized text filter, including the focus and event-stopping bugs that were found.
executive_summary: This document walks through three pieces of AG Grid integration code: an initializeSelect2() utility, a CustomSelectEditor that wraps Select2 inside an AG Grid popup editor, and a CustomTextFilter that fully replaces AG Grid's default text filter with Portuguese labels and dictionary-aware filtering. It explains every method, every config option, and flags four real bugs in the editor (e.g. the global $('.select2-search__field') selector that hijacks focus across all instances). It is essentially a code-archaeology pass on the FactoryFloor grid layer.

tutorial_structure.why_it_exists: FactoryFloor's grids needed dropdown editors that look up names from in-memory dictionaries (motoristas, viaturas, servicos) instead of showing raw IDs, plus a filter that searches against those human-readable names while keeping Portuguese terminology. The default AG Grid editor and filter couldn't do that, so Select2 was bolted on and a custom filter was written.
tutorial_structure.what_it_does: initializeSelect2() converts every <select class='select2'> on the page into a Select2 dropdown with Portuguese localization. CustomSelectEditor builds a wrapper div, populates a <select> from params.values mapped through a context dictionary, then calls Select2 inside a setTimeout. CustomTextFilter constructs an AG-Grid-styled filter UI with a six-option dropdown (contains/equals/startsWith/etc.), a magnifying-glass input, and a 'Limpar Filtro' button; doesFilterPass converts array columns (servicosIds, viaturasIds) into searchable strings via dictionary lookup before applying the chosen comparison.
tutorial_structure.how_it_works: The editor stores parameters, creates DOM elements imperatively, and chooses idToNameMap based on params.column.colDef.field. Select2 is initialized with dropdownParent: document.body (flagged as a problem because it breaks focus management). The filter implements AG Grid's lifecycle: init, getGui, isFilterActive, doesFilterPass, getModel/setModel for state restoration, and event handlers that call params.filterChangedCallback() to retrigger the grid. doesFilterPass case-insensitively compares with the cell value, joining array columns via dictionary[id]?.Nome before running the switch on filterType.

suggested_metaphor: Think of AG Grid's editor and filter slots like USB ports on a motherboard: AG Grid promises to deliver power and data to whatever you plug in, as long as your component implements the contract (init, getGui, getValue...). Select2 isn't a USB device though, it's an old serial peripheral, so this code is the adapter cable wrapping a vintage jQuery plugin in a USB shell, complete with the loose wires that make focus jump to the wrong window when the dog walks past.
suggested_intro_hook: Why does focus keep jumping to the wrong dropdown when you have three Select2 editors open in a grid? Because somewhere, someone wrote $('.select2-search__field').focus() and that selector finds every Select2 search field on the page. This document is what happens when you finally sit down and read your own code.
what_it_teaches: How to implement AG Grid's custom editor and filter contracts in vanilla JavaScript, how to integrate the legacy Select2 jQuery plugin with a modern grid, how dictionary-backed lookups make filters search by display name rather than ID, and how subtle global selectors and dropdownParent settings can break focus.
key_takeaways: AG Grid editors must implement init, getGui, getValue, isPopup, destroy and optionally onKeyDown/afterGuiAttached
Filters need init, getGui, isFilterActive, doesFilterPass, getModel, setModel and a filterChangedCallback to refresh the grid
Global jQuery selectors like $('.select2-search__field') will steal focus across multiple component instances
Array columns can be made searchable by joining dictionary lookups into a single string before doesFilterPass runs the comparison
dropdownParent: document.body breaks AG Grid's focus management because the dropdown escapes the editor container
quality_notes: Very thorough method-by-method walkthrough with explicit bug callouts (PROBLEM #1 through #4). The PDF table of contents mid-document is a bit messy but the actual content is complete. The companion DOCX in this same batch covers the same material with cleaner formatting.

title: Select2 + jQuery Document Ready - Method Breakdown and AG Grid Custom Editor/Filter
one_line_summary: A cleaned-up DOCX twin of the Select2/AG Grid PDF walkthrough, covering initializeSelect2(), the jQuery document-ready pattern, and the same CustomSelectEditor and CustomTextFilter classes with the same bug callouts.
executive_summary: This document is the markdown-clean version of the FactoryFloor Select2 + AG Grid integration walkthrough. It teaches what jQuery(document).ready(function ($) { ... }) actually does (parameter mapping the full jQuery object to a local $), why initializeSelect2() guards against missing libraries, and walks every method of CustomSelectEditor and CustomTextFilter while flagging four bugs in the editor. The filter analysis is slightly less detailed than the PDF version (no array/dictionary handling section in doesFilterPass), but the editor walkthrough is identical.

tutorial_structure.why_it_exists: FactoryFloor uses AG Grid for editing schedules and lookup-heavy tables. The default editors don't handle the dictionary-to-display-name pattern that the app needs, so the team built a Select2-backed editor and a custom text filter with Portuguese labels. This document was written to demystify that code for whoever reads it next.
tutorial_structure.what_it_does: Explains the jQuery document-ready safety dance, then dissects three classes/utilities: initializeSelect2() applies Portuguese-localized Select2 to all .select2 elements; CustomSelectEditor builds a 200px wrapper, a populated <select>, and bolts Select2 on top with a setTimeout; CustomTextFilter constructs a complete AG-Grid-styled filter UI with dropdown, search input, and clear button.
tutorial_structure.how_it_works: The walkthrough goes section-by-section through every method, showing what AG Grid calls when (init -> getGui -> afterGuiAttached -> getValue -> destroy), explains state restoration via getModel/setModel, and shows how event handlers wire .bind(this) so the filter instance is preserved. Four issues are flagged in the editor: dropdownParent: document.body, the broad e.stopPropagation(), the global $('.select2-search__field') focus selector, and opening Select2 inside afterGuiAttached before initialization is guaranteed.

suggested_metaphor: jQuery's document-ready is like a polite party guest who waits in the hallway until the host has finished arranging the chairs before walking in and starting conversations. Without it, your script kicks down the door at midnight and tries to chat up furniture that hasn't been delivered yet.
suggested_intro_hook: Why does jQuery(document).ready(function ($) { ... }) take $ as a parameter when $ is already global? Because somebody else's library might have stolen $ before you got there, and that local parameter is your private re-rental contract on the shorthand.
what_it_teaches: How AG Grid's plug-in points work, how to integrate jQuery plugins (Select2) inside a modern grid lifecycle, why the document-ready pattern uses $ as a parameter, and how to spot bugs that come from global selectors and event-stopping that's too broad.
key_takeaways: jQuery(document).ready takes $ as a parameter to guarantee the local shorthand maps to jQuery even if other libraries hijacked the global
AG Grid follows a strict editor lifecycle (init, getGui, afterGuiAttached, getValue, destroy, isPopup, onKeyDown)
Custom filters must implement init, getGui, doesFilterPass, isFilterActive, getModel, and setModel
Calling .bind(this) on event handlers preserves the component instance for AG Grid filters
Stopping all events on a Select2 container is too broad - it blocks AG Grid's own click handling
quality_notes: Cleaner than the PDF twin and arguably easier to read, but the doesFilterPass section is the older version that doesn't handle array columns via dictionary lookup. If you want the array-handling logic, read the PDF version. Both are valuable as a pair.

title: Database Reset & Tenant Migration - How GivingCare Provisions Its Databases
one_line_summary: Walks through GivingCare's two-database (Auth + per-tenant Company) architecture, the TenantMigrator utility, and the SQL reset script that wipes everything so EF Core can rebuild from scratch with seed data.
executive_summary: This document explains how GivingCare 3.0 provisions, seeds, and resets its multi-tenant SQL Server databases. It covers the BaseControleContext (one Auth DB) vs DynamicCompanyContext (one DB per tenant) split, what MigrateAsync() actually does step by step (creates DB, manages __EFMigrationsHistory, applies pending migrations, runs HasData seeds), the three command-line flags exposed by Program.cs (--migrate-all, --migrate-auth, --migrate-tenants), and the SQL reset script that uses SET SINGLE_USER WITH ROLLBACK IMMEDIATE to forcibly drop databases. It also explains design-time vs runtime context creation and how to add a new tenant.

tutorial_structure.why_it_exists: GivingCare needed a deterministic, repeatable way to reset development environments and to provision new tenant databases. Drift between dev machines and broken seed data were causing 'works on my machine' bugs, and the team needed a single command that wipes everything and rebuilds from migrations.
tutorial_structure.what_it_does: The TenantMigrator static class exposes MigrateAuthDatabaseAsync, MigrateTenantAsync(key), MigrateTenantsAsync, and MigrateAllAsync. Program.cs checks for --migrate-all, --migrate-auth, or --migrate-tenants in the args and runs the corresponding method then return; (it does NOT start the web server). The companion SQL script in Scripts/ResetDatabases.sql drops the AuthDatabase and every company database, after which a single dotnet run -- --migrate-all rebuilds them with seed data.
tutorial_structure.how_it_works: MigrateAsync() compares migrations in code against __EFMigrationsHistory rows and applies anything missing. HasData() in OnModelCreating requires explicit primary key values (Id = 1) so EF can track seed data across migrations. The auth DB seeds a SuperAdmin (agile/1234, ChangePassword=true), 4 SystemRoles, 100+ permissions, and Geography. Each company DB seeds 13 doc types, state configs, and 56+ employee permissions. Design-time factories implement IDesignTimeDbContextFactory<BaseControleContext> so dotnet ef migrations add can build a context without DI. The reset script uses ALTER DATABASE ... SET SINGLE_USER WITH ROLLBACK IMMEDIATE to kick out connections, then DROP DATABASE.

suggested_metaphor: GivingCare's database setup is an apartment building. The AuthDatabase is the lobby with the master key cabinet, the resident registry, and the directory of which apartment numbers exist. Each Company DB is a furnished apartment - same floor plan (schema), totally different furniture (data). The TenantMigrator is the building superintendent who can rebuild the lobby alone, refurnish a single apartment, or bulldoze the whole building and put it up again from blueprints (migrations) and the catalog (seed data).
suggested_intro_hook: Why does running dotnet run -- --migrate-all twice in a row do nothing the second time? Because MigrateAsync() looks at __EFMigrationsHistory before doing anything, and that little tracking table is the difference between idempotent setup and a corruption disaster. Read on to see what really happens when EF Core 'migrates' your database.
what_it_teaches: How EF Core migrations work end-to-end (the history table, idempotency, seed data via HasData), how to architect a multi-tenant app with one auth database and many company databases, why design-time DbContext factories exist, and how to write a reset script that won't fail on missing databases.
key_takeaways: Two databases, two contexts: AuthDatabase (BaseControleContext) is shared, Company DBs (DynamicCompanyContext) are per-tenant
MigrateAsync() is idempotent because it uses __EFMigrationsHistory to skip already-applied migrations
Migration commands use return; after running so they exit without starting the web server
Auth must be migrated before company databases because the Companies table lives in auth
HasData() requires explicit primary keys so EF can track seed rows across migrations
ALTER DATABASE ... SET SINGLE_USER WITH ROLLBACK IMMEDIATE is how you force-drop a database with active connections
Design-time factories let dotnet ef migrations add work without a DI container or running app
quality_notes: Excellent - this is one of the highest-quality documents in the library. Includes diagrams, comparison tables, callout metaphors, and walks through both the why and the how. Already self-contained as its own HTML page with custom styling and 'Read It Like English' callouts.

title: Sistema de Serviço de Stock - O Guia Para Totós
one_line_summary: Beginner-friendly Portuguese walkthrough of a cached IStockService that uses the decorator pattern, time-based cache expiration, and pre-loading to make inventory lookups feel instant.
executive_summary: This is the Portuguese 'Para Totós' (For Dummies) guide to the Stock Service. It explains the two-layer architecture (CachedStockService decorating StockService), the brilliant time-based cache strategy (1 hour for historical data >7 days old, 5 minutes for recent data, no caching for filtered queries), and the four core methods: GetArticleStockByDateAsync (time machine), GetStockMovementsAsync (history book), GetStockTotalsAsync (summary), and CheckFluxoAsync (special inspector). It also covers the UI pre-loading trick in ArtigoDetalhe.razor where _stockSummaryTask starts loading in OnInitializedAsync before the user even clicks the Stock tab.

tutorial_structure.why_it_exists: Inventory checks were slow because every stock query meant counting movements from the database, and the same questions were being asked repeatedly by different users. The team needed sub-second responses without forcing the database to do the same SUM(entradas - saidas) calculation 50 times per minute.
tutorial_structure.what_it_does: Wraps the real StockService in a CachedStockService that uses IMemoryCache with a smart time-based expiration policy. Historical data (more than 7 days old) is cached for 1 hour because old stock numbers don't change. Recent data is cached for only 5 minutes because today's numbers might still move. Filtered queries (date ranges, specific docs) skip the cache entirely because they're too unique to repeat. The Razor page pre-loads stock data in OnInitializedAsync so by the time the user clicks the Stock tab, the result is already waiting.
tutorial_structure.how_it_works: CachedStockService.GetArticleStockByDateAsync builds a cache key like stock_{artigoId}_{date:yyyyMMdd}, checks _cache.TryGetValue first, falls through to _innerService.GetArticleStockByDateAsync if missed, then writes back with TimeSpan.FromHours(1) or TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5) depending on the date. The underlying SQL is a SUM over entradas/saidas with a +1 day trick to include all movements on the boundary date. ArtigoDetalhe.razor stores _stockSummaryTask = StockService.GetCurrentStockAsync(artigo.Id) in OnInitializedAsync, then the OnStockTabClick handler just awaits that already-running task. DI is wired so IStockService resolves to CachedStockService wrapping a concrete StockService.

suggested_metaphor: This stock service is like having post-it notes on your desk for the questions people ask you most. The first time someone asks 'what's João's phone number?' you flip through the phone book and write the answer on a post-it. Next time? You just read the post-it. And because phone numbers from last year never change but today's might still get updated, you keep old post-its for an hour and new ones for only five minutes.
suggested_intro_hook: What if your inventory page could show today's stock levels in 0.001 seconds instead of 2 seconds, without writing a single line of new SQL? The trick isn't speed - it's memory. This is the story of how a decorator and an IMemoryCache turned a slow service into one that pretends to be psychic.
what_it_teaches: How the decorator pattern lets you add caching without touching the original service, how to choose cache expiration windows based on how stable the data is, how task pre-loading can make UIs feel instant, and how to register a decorated service in .NET's DI container.
key_takeaways: The decorator pattern lets you add caching as a transparent wrapper without modifying the original service
Cache expiration should match data volatility: longer for historical data, shorter for recent, none for filtered queries
Task pre-loading in OnInitializedAsync makes tab clicks feel instant because the work happens during render time
Cache keys should encode every parameter that affects the answer (article ID + date in this case)
DI registration for decorated services uses a factory delegate that resolves the inner service then wraps it
GetStockTotalsAsync only caches the unfiltered totals - filtered queries skip cache because they're too unique to repeat
quality_notes: Excellent beginner-friendly tone with strong analogies (post-its, phone book, time machine). Portuguese language. The Para Totós format makes this very accessible. Has multiple architecture diagrams in ASCII and concrete code samples. This is the PT counterpart to the English Stock service docs.

title: Generic Schedule Grid - For Dummies
one_line_summary: Refactoring story of a 2000-line Razor schedule grid into a single GenericScheduleGrid<TSchedule> backed by four IScheduleGridDataProvider implementations - one component, four views, no copy-paste.
executive_summary: This document describes how the team turned what would have been four near-identical 2000-line Razor schedule components (Job to Employees, Job to Equipment, Employee to Jobs, Equipment to Jobs) into a single generic GenericScheduleGrid<TSchedule> component. The grid delegates data fetching and saving to an injected IScheduleGridDataProvider, and each of the four views supplies its own provider. Rows implement IScheduleGridRow so the grid can render Employees, Equipment, or Jobs uniformly without knowing what they are. Schedules implement IScheduleEntry so the grid can compute hours and detect overlaps generically. Adding a fifth view (Team -> Employees) means writing one provider and one wrapper - no changes to the grid itself.

tutorial_structure.why_it_exists: The team had a beautiful schedule grid showing Employees on Jobs but needed three more views: Equipment on Jobs, Jobs on Employee, and Jobs on Equipment. The naive copy-paste approach would have produced 8000+ lines to maintain, with bug fixes and feature requests needing four touches each. They needed one component that worked for all four perspectives.
tutorial_structure.what_it_does: GenericScheduleGrid<TSchedule> renders a row-and-column schedule editor where the rows can be any IScheduleGridRow, the cells contain any IScheduleEntry, and all data fetching is delegated to an injected IScheduleGridDataProvider<TSchedule>. Four data providers (JobEmployeeScheduleDataProvider, JobEquipmentScheduleDataProvider, EmployeeJobScheduleDataProvider, EquipmentJobScheduleDataProvider) each know how to ask the database for the rows and schedules of one specific perspective. Thin wrapper components (JobEmployeeScheduleTab, JobEquipmentScheduleTab, EmployeeScheduleTab, EquipmentScheduleTab) just configure the generic grid with the right provider and ContextId.
tutorial_structure.how_it_works: The IScheduleGridDataProvider<TSchedule> contract requires GetRowsAsync, GetSchedulesAsync, CreateNewSchedule, and CRUD methods. JobEmployeeScheduleDataProvider's GetRowsAsync queries JobEmployee where JobId == jobId; EmployeeJobScheduleDataProvider's GetRowsAsync queries the same join table but filtered by EmployeeId. IScheduleGridRow exposes RowId, RowLabel, RowIcon, NavigationUrl so the grid can render any entity uniformly. IScheduleEntry exposes ScheduleDate, CheckInTime, CheckOutTime, IsCrossMidnightShift, OverlapsWith() so the grid can compute hours and warn about conflicts without caring whether it's an employee or equipment schedule. Adding a new view is four steps: write the provider, register it in DI, write a wrapper that injects it, drop it on the page.

suggested_metaphor: GenericScheduleGrid is like a universal picture frame that doesn't care what painting you put in it - oil, watercolor, photograph, child's crayon drawing - it just needs the painting to have a width, a height, and a way to hang. The data providers are the curators who know which paintings live in which gallery and how to take them off the wall, while the wrapper components are the gallery labels that say 'this frame currently shows the Renaissance collection.'
suggested_intro_hook: How do you avoid maintaining 8000 lines of copy-pasted Razor when business asks for the same grid 'but inverted'? You stop writing components for entities and start writing components for shapes. This is the story of how four schedule views became one generic grid plus four 30-line wrappers.
what_it_teaches: How to use C# generics with Razor components, how to apply the strategy pattern via DI to remove code duplication, how interface abstractions (IScheduleGridRow, IScheduleEntry) let one UI render multiple entity types, and how to extend a system by writing a new provider rather than a new component.
key_takeaways: When you find yourself about to copy-paste a component, look for a generic type parameter and a strategy interface instead
Wrapper components should be thin - just inject a provider and configure the generic component
Interfaces like IScheduleGridRow let totally different entities (Employees, Equipment, Jobs) be rendered by the same UI code
ContextId is the 'fixed axis' (the entity the user is viewing), RowId is what appears in each row
Adding a new view should mean writing a provider, not modifying the generic component
Razor supports generic type parameters via TSchedule, making this pattern work in markup
quality_notes: Excellent For Dummies-style writing with concrete file paths, before/after comparisons, and a step-by-step example of adding a new view (Teams -> Employees). The ASCII diagrams clarify the relationship between the grid and the providers. Numbered '09-' suggests this is part of a series.

title: Async Pattern - Task.WhenAll, Cold Tasks, and Awaiting Existing Tasks
one_line_summary: Walkthrough of a Microsoft async example showing how to start two tasks before awaiting them, and the rule that calling a method creates a task while awaiting an existing task does not re-run it.
executive_summary: This document teaches the difference between starting an async task and awaiting it, using a small Microsoft Product/Review fetch example. The key insight is that Task<List<Product>> productsTask = FetchProductsAsync() starts the work immediately and returns a handle, so two tasks started back-to-back run in parallel; await Task.WhenAll(productsTask, reviewsTask) then waits for both, taking max(2s, 3s) = 3 seconds instead of 5 seconds sequential. It also clarifies the rule that calling FetchProductsAsync() creates a new task each time, but await existingTask just waits for the same task without re-running the method. Includes a second example with DoOtherWork() interleaved between starting and awaiting.
suggested_metaphor: Starting two tasks then awaiting Task.WhenAll is like placing two food delivery orders at the same time and then sitting down to wait. If you order pizza first and stand at the door until it arrives before ordering sushi, you wait pizza-time + sushi-time. If you order both then sit down, you wait max(pizza-time, sushi-time). And awaiting a task you've already stored is like checking your delivery app - you're not re-ordering, just looking at the status of the order that's already on the way.
suggested_intro_hook: What's the difference between 'await this method' and 'await this task variable'? One starts the work, the other just waits for work that's already running. Get this wrong and you turn your parallel async code back into sequential code without realizing it.
what_it_teaches: How to start async work concurrently by storing the returned Task before awaiting, why Task.WhenAll runs tasks in parallel (max time, not sum), and the critical distinction that calling FetchAsync() always starts new work but await existingTask never re-runs the method.
key_takeaways: Calling an async method returns a Task that starts running immediately - it's not a recipe, it's a running pot
Storing tasks then awaiting them with Task.WhenAll runs them in parallel; sequential awaits run them serially
await existingTask does NOT re-run the method - it just waits for the result of the already-running task
Two consecutive Fetch...Async() calls produce two independent running tasks
Total time with Task.WhenAll is max(durations), not sum(durations)
Forgetting to await a task can swallow exceptions silently
quality_notes: Short and effective. Uses two clear examples (Microsoft Product/Review and a custom DoWorkAsync) to make the cold-vs-hot distinction stick. Light on concepts like SynchronizationContext or ConfigureAwait, which is fine for a beginner intro. Mixes English and one Portuguese label ('Exemplo do Gepeto').

title: Role-Based Authorization - From Boolean Flags to Hierarchical Roles
one_line_summary: Migration guide from inline boolean role flags (IsSuperAdmin, IsAdmin, IsManager) to a database-driven SystemRole table with numeric Levels that enable hierarchical 'admin or above' checks.
executive_summary: This document explains why GivingCare moved away from boolean role flags on the User entity (IsSuperAdmin, IsAdmin, IsManager) and toward a SystemRole table with a numeric Level column (100/80/60/40). The numeric levels enable elegant hierarchical checks like RoleLevel >= 80 meaning 'admin or above'. AuthorizationService.GetUserRoleAsync returns the highest active role for a user, AuthenticatedComponentBase exposes IsSuperAdmin/IsAdminOrAbove/IsManagerOrAbove convenience properties, and CanAssignRoleAsync enforces that admins can only assign roles below their own. Includes a migration cheat sheet for translating old user.IsAdmin checks into the new pattern.

tutorial_structure.why_it_exists: The old pattern stored IsSuperAdmin, IsAdmin, IsManager as bools directly on the User entity. This made it impossible to express 'admin or above', forced schema changes for every new role, gave no audit trail of who assigned which role, and could leave a user inconsistently flagged as both admin and manager. The team needed something that scaled and was auditable.
tutorial_structure.what_it_does: Defines a SystemRole table with Id, Code, and Level columns (SuperAdmin=100, Admin=80, Manager=60, User=40), plus a UserSystemRole join table that records who has which role. AuthorizationService.GetUserRoleAsync queries the join, picks the highest Level for the user, and maps it to a UserRole enum. AuthenticatedComponentBase loads the role in OnInitializedAsync and exposes IsSuperAdmin/IsAdminOrAbove/IsManagerOrAbove properties so Razor pages can do @if (IsAdminOrAbove) { ... }. CanAssignRoleAsync enforces that you can only assign roles strictly below your own.
tutorial_structure.how_it_works: GetUserRoleAsync joins UserSystemRoles to SystemRole, filters by IsActive, orders by Level descending, takes the first, and returns the corresponding UserRole enum value via a switch on Level. AuthenticatedComponentBase stores the result in CurrentUserRole and RoleLevel. Razor pages inherit the base and use IsAdminOrAbove instead of querying the database. CanAssignRoleAsync uses a switch on the assigner's role: SuperAdmin can assign anything, Admin can assign Manager or below, Manager can only assign Regular users.

suggested_metaphor: Boolean role flags are like a coatroom where each coat has a sticker that says 'gold member' or 'silver member' or 'bronze member' - you have to check every sticker to know who's most senior. The hierarchical Level approach is like giving every coat a number from 0 to 100 - now 'gold or above' is just 'number >= 80' and you don't need to enumerate every tier individually.
suggested_intro_hook: How do you check 'is this user admin or above' when your User class has separate IsAdmin and IsManager bool flags? The honest answer is: with a tangle of OR conditions that breaks every time someone adds a new role. There's a better way, and it's just one numeric column.
what_it_teaches: Why boolean role flags are a maintenance trap, how to model roles as a separate table with numeric Levels, how to expose role checks via an inheritable Blazor base component, and how to enforce role-assignment hierarchy server-side.
key_takeaways: Boolean role flags on User make 'role or above' checks ugly and force schema changes for every new role
A SystemRole table with a numeric Level column enables clean hierarchical checks like Level >= 80
AuthenticatedComponentBase loads the role once in OnInitializedAsync and exposes IsAdminOrAbove convenience properties
CanAssignRoleAsync should enforce that you can only assign roles strictly below your own level
OrderByDescending(Level).FirstOrDefault gives you the highest active role for a user
Database-driven roles enable an audit trail of who assigned which role to whom
quality_notes: Short and clear, focused tightly on the role refactoring story. Includes a migration cheat sheet table mapping old patterns to new ones. Could benefit from a sequence diagram and a discussion of how this interacts with ASP.NET Core's built-in authorization policies, but as a focused refactoring writeup it's complete.
